narr.Muddle Through:
Status-quo extension of the post-demerger franchise: mining-customer demand holds, input costs are broadly stable, and the US cost-curve advantage from long-term gas contracts is intact in the near term. The single most consequential firm-specific variable — the US gas-contract roll-off in the 2028–2030 window — is built explicitly into the margin path (−50/−100/−150 bps cumulative Y3/Y4/Y5), and is offset by peer-gap closure toward Orica-level efficiency.

Why AUD 3.48? It sits modestly below market (AUD 3.61, ~4%) — the framework agrees with consensus on the central case. The value-add is not disagreement here, it is the scenario asymmetry around this point.

Mental short-cut: a cyclical industrial priced fairly at the centre, but with a downside that bites ~4× harder than the upside lifts.
narr.Orderly Convergence: Mining capex healthy, transition-mineral demand (copper, lithium, nickel) pulls volumes, and a modest margin lift comes through. The upside is real but capped by the oligopolistic structure — only +AUD 0.57 above Muddle Through.
narr.AI Productivity Lag: Close to neutral. A modest labour-cost benefit on SG&A from automation, otherwise the macro is broadly status-quo. −3% vs Muddle Through — the least-sensitive scenario.
narr.Fragmentation: DNL sits ~90% in the US-aligned bloc (USA + Australia), which is the slower-growing bloc; cross-bloc ammonium-nitrate and ammonia flows are regulatorily sensitive and supply chains duplicate. Partially offset by Australia’s strategic-mineral position. −27%.
narr.Disorderly Climate: Coal customers (~35% of the mix) attrit faster than the standard fade assumes; carbon costs flow through ammonia into bulk ANFO; capex rises. A partial offset from transition-mineral mining demand. The moat decays over a shortened fade (§10.6). −60%.
narr.Stagflation Persists: The binding downside. Sustained input-cost inflation that cannot be passed through — supplier power blocks it while mining customers resist price increases — combined with slowing mining capex. −65% vs Muddle Through; the −AUD 2.31 that sets the 4.05× asymmetry.

dnl._position:
• Pure-play post-demerger – explosives-only after the March 2025 Incitec Pivot split (fertilisers demerged, entity renamed); single reporting segment.
  • Global #2, Australian duopolist – #1 in North American industrial explosives (~30% share), #2 to Orica in Australia (~40% share), plus a sub-scale ~5% RoW book slowly gaining.
  • Geography & currency – ~55% USA, ~35% Australia, ~10% RoW; per-entity functional currency under IAS 21 (parent AUD, Dyno Nobel Americas USD-functional on US revenue, gas and ammonia).
  • US cost-curve edge – transitory – long-term gas contracts put US ops in the bottom cost-curve quartile (~+200bps margin), rolling off through a 2028–2030 re-pricing window (6-year average maturity) to nil by FY31.
  • Switching-cost moat – 200+ on-site mobile manufacturing units at customer mine sites, multi-decade relationships and 5–10-year offtake contracts (BHP, Rio Tinto, FMG); ~78% of revenue contracted.
  • Product & customer mix – ~50% commodity bulk ANFO, ~18% higher-growth electronic detonators (DigiShot); ~35% coal-exposed, offset by transition-mineral demand. Top 5 customers ~45% of revenue.
  • Peer-gap to Orica – Orica is ~30% larger with a technology and diversification lead, driving a net ~25bps company-position growth drag (−30 rivalry, −10 mix, +15 EM ramp).
  • Key risks – gas/ammonia input costs, coal-customer transition, and a weak large-project execution record (Louisiana ammonia overruns 2017–2020); carbon exposure rated high given ~55% ammonia self-supply.
  • Balance sheet – net debt/EBITDA 2.12x; AUD 647m liquidity; thin FY25 free cash flow (AUD 101m) vs AUD 162m dividends + AUD 289m buybacks; 60–70% payout target.

worldDesc.Muddle Through: Post-2022 friction proves persistent rather than transitional: inflation cools but lands above target (2.5–3.5%) and central banks tacitly accept the overshoot rather than crush demand. Real rates settle structurally higher than the 2010s (~1.0%). The US keeps outperforming on fiscal expansion, AI investment and immigration, but the lift doesn’t propagate to Europe or EM. Climate policy stays patchy and AI’s productivity transmission is slow, with rents concentrating in platform owners. No crisis, no resolution — a grinding extension of present conditions. Global growth ~2.3%.
worldDesc.Orderly Convergence: The conditions for benign resolution stack up at once. Supply-side normalisation plus genuine AI productivity gains absorb wage pressure, so inflation returns to ~2.3% without a demand crush; real rates settle modestly positive. The political reset climate policy needed happens, and geopolitical tensions materially de-escalate. This time US growth propagates — pulling Europe out of stagnation and supporting EM — and AI rents diffuse, re-expanding growth multiples. Global growth recovers to 3.0–3.2%.
worldDesc.Stagflation Persists: The IMF severe scenario plays out: an energy shock spikes prices and keeps them elevated, inflation expectations break above the 3% credibility threshold, and second-round wage-price dynamics take hold. Central banks lose credibility and hold restrictive policy through the horizon; real rates settle 2–3% with recession inside the scenario. Climate policy backslides as a cost-of-living crisis crushes the transition coalition; growth-stock multiples compress and trade barriers ratchet up. Growth slows to 1.5–2.0%.
worldDesc.Fragmentation: The US-China contest hardens and trade-as-weapon (tariffs, sanctions, export controls) becomes routine, extending into industrial and commodity flows. Supply chains regionalise into duplicated US-aligned and China-aligned systems, energy markets bifurcate, and critical-minerals access becomes the new geopolitical front. The duplicated footprint is inflationary (~3.5%) and growth bifurcates — China-aligned economies may outpace the US-aligned bloc, with Europe hit hardest and Australia facing an acute security-vs-supply dilemma. The new equilibrium is structurally inferior.
worldDesc.Disorderly Climate: The already-running disorderly climate path has its crystallisation moment — most likely a confluence of a catastrophic insured-loss event, regulator-forced de-leveraging of carbon-intensive loan books, and a carbon-price spike. Policy snaps from drift to abrupt crisis action: carbon prices to EUR 200+, border-adjustment mechanisms, expanded transition subsidies. Capital reallocates abruptly, so sectoral dispersion widens sharply even as aggregate growth stays near Muddle Through (~2.0–2.2%, inflation 4.5–5% from carbon pass-through). This scenario tests terminal-state convergence hardest — assumed-perpetual moats reveal stranded-asset half-lives inside the horizon.
worldDesc.AI Productivity Lag: The Solow paradox at AI scale. Capability and capex advance genuinely (deficit-funded, US-led), but economy-wide productivity transformation doesn’t arrive on the bull timeline: enterprise adoption is slow, so aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5% versus the 1.5%+ current investment implies. Rents capture is asymmetric — platform owners take the bulk while broad enterprise pays without proportional payback — and market concentration intensifies. The saving grace is the labour-cost channel: AI contains white-collar wage growth even where productivity transmission is weak. Headline numbers resemble Muddle Through, but the underlying story differs.

_drtheory: Risk-free rate

A long-dated government bond yield in the cash-flow currency, ideally matched to the horizon/duration of the cash flows. Practice splits between the deep, liquid 10-year benchmark and a term-matched long bond for very long-life assets; a single YTM is only an average and distorts NPV when the curve is steep. Most take a recent spot rate rather than a normalised one.

In practice, valuers use a recent spot yield on a long government bond in the cash-flow currency — most commonly the 10-year, though some duration-match to 20 or 30-year bonds for very long-life assets. Normalising the rate is debated but usually set aside in favour of a current market yield.
10-year Commonwealth Government Securities YTM, 4.30% (indicative, May 2026). Single spot 10-year — the pragmatic-benchmark choice, no duration-matching or normalisation.
Equity risk premium

The unobservable expected excess return of equities over the risk-free asset, estimated from long-run historical premia, forward-looking/implied models, or surveys — none theoretically superior. Convention has settled near 6.0%, while acknowledging large statistical error.

Independent experts and practitioners typically adopt a market risk premium around 6.0% (a 5–7% range is common), close to updated long-run historical estimates. The estimate carries very wide statistical error — the true premium behind a measured 6% could plausibly sit anywhere in a 2–10% band — and Australian practice usually makes no explicit imputation adjustment inside it.
5.0% — a Damodaran-style mature-Australia premium, deliberately ~100bps below the 6.0% Australian-expert convention, with a small country premium baked in.
Beta

Raw single-stock regression beta is noisy and window-dependent, so triangulate from a comparable set: unlever peer equity betas to asset betas and re-lever to a target structure, and/or use adjusted (mean-reverting) or fundamental betas. Index choice (local vs global) and estimation window materially change the answer.

Standard practice is to triangulate from a comparable set rather than trust a single regression: a subject’s measured beta can swing widely across data providers and estimation windows (often anywhere from ~0.8 to ~2.7 for the same company), so experts lean on adjusted / fundamental betas and peer clusters, and treat mechanical unlever / relever with caution.
Peer triangulation, rejecting the measured 0.36 (unreliable post-demerger): Orica ~1.05 / Yara ~1.20 / ICL ~1.10 cluster (Sasol 1.45 excluded) → selected 1.10.
Cost of debt / debt margin

Risk-free rate plus a debt margin set by the company’s (or comparable-set) credit rating, referencing traded corporate-bond spreads over sovereigns at matching tenor; use a target rating consistent with the assumed gearing, not just the current coupon.

Cost of debt is normally built as the risk-free rate plus a credit-rating-based margin — a BBB issuer’s traded spread over the sovereign at matching tenor, using a target rating consistent with the assumed gearing rather than the current coupon. Margins of ~1.5–3% over the risk-free rate are typical for investment-grade names.
6.00% pre-tax = an AUD investment-grade BBB-tier spread (~170bps) over the 10-year sovereign; after-tax 6.00% × (1−0.30) = 4.20%.
Gearing / capital-structure weights

Weight equity and debt at market value, using a target/through-cycle structure informed by the subject’s own gearing plus the comparable-set average, rather than a single spot snapshot (which is volatile and often inconsistent with the betas measured over the same window).

Weights are taken at market value on a target / through-cycle basis, informed by the comparable-set average rather than a single spot snapshot — commonly 15–25% debt for capital-light industrials, higher for infrastructure-like assets.
Market-value weights E/V 79% / D/V 21% (equity = 1,884m shares × AUD 3.61; debt = reported net debt). Market-value basis using reported net debt.
Gamma / imputation credits

Australia’s dividend-imputation system gives resident investors franking credits; some argue these should be captured via a ‘gamma’ factor (contested, ~0.25–0.65). Regulators such as the AER apply it through the tax line.

Whether to capture franking credits (via a ‘gamma’ factor, contested at ~0.25–0.65) is heavily debated. Many independent valuers decline to adjust for imputation in a business-valuation context, arguing credit value is effectively binary across the shareholder base (full value to some domestic investors, nil to foreign ones) and not reliably priced by the market.
Not applied — consistent with the standard business-valuation view, and with our ERP making no explicit imputation allowance.
WACC vs cost of equity

For an industrial/miner, discount ungeared after-tax cash flows at a WACC, then bridge enterprise value to equity via net debt. For a bank, debt is raw material (deposits/wholesale funding are operating inputs), so discount cash flows to equity at the cost of equity directly — a WACC/EV bridge is wrong.

Industrials and miners are valued by discounting ungeared after-tax cash flows at a WACC and bridging to equity via net debt; concluded WACCs for mature resource / industrial businesses commonly land around 7–9% (higher in higher-risk jurisdictions). Banks are the exception — deposits and wholesale funding are operating inputs, so bank cash flows are discounted to equity at the cost of equity directly, with no WACC / EV bridge.
WACC ≈ 8.68% (Re 9.80% at β 1.10; 79% equity + 21% debt at 4.20% after-tax). Held constant across scenarios (§3.5).

narr.Muddle Through:
Status-quo extension: NIM held at the through-cycle 1.94% anchor, the UNITE cost-to-income glide delivers part of the peer-gap closure, and credit losses run at the 18 bps through-cycle anchor. CET1 (12.42%) sits comfortably above target, supporting the buyback.

Why AUD 30.15, ~15% below market? The market (AUD 35.32) is implicitly trading WBC at a successful-transformation outcome — essentially the Orderly Convergence scenario (AUD 35.46) — not at this status-quo base. To converge to market on a Muddle Through path, terminal ROE has to be 12.1% (CBA-like), not the archetype mid-point.

Mental short-cut: the market is paying for the transformation; Muddle Through is what you get if it only half-lands.
narr.Orderly Convergence: Healthy loan growth, a benign credit cycle and modest NIM uplift; UNITE closes most of the cost-to-income gap. At AUD 35.46 it sits essentially at market — the framework’s read on what current pricing implies. +17.6% vs Muddle Through.
narr.AI Productivity Lag: Close to neutral. A modest cost benefit from automation, offset by weaker macro loan demand. −1.3% vs Muddle Through.
narr.Fragmentation: Hits non-interest income (markets / institutional) more than net interest income, with modest credit losses on the business book. −9.5%.
narr.Disorderly Climate: APRA climate-adjusted RWA models lift capital intensity for vulnerable zones; WBC’s #2 mortgage book carries more absolute climate-vulnerable exposure than NAB or ANZ. Transmission is mainly via terminal-ROE compression (−1.5pp). −23%.
narr.Stagflation Persists: The binding downside. NIM compresses −20 bps (deposit competition + slow front-book repricing), credit losses lift to peak-cycle (+50 bps), and cost growth runs ahead of the glide. CET1 forces payout from 75% down to ~50% to rebuild capital. NPAT Y5 AUD 3.7bn vs MT AUD 8.9bn. −33%.

• #2 Big Four franchise – second-largest by total assets, anchored on a AUD 517.7bn Australian mortgage book (~20% system share, #2 to CBA’s ~25%) plus an AUD 18.5bn RAMS book in run-off.
  • Deposit-funded edge – #2 household deposits (AUD 615bn retail base), including AUD 149bn non-interest-bearing transaction balances giving a structural +8bps NIM funding-cost advantage over wholesale-funded peers.
  • Segment mix – consumer ~37% of earnings, business & wealth ~28% (AUD 238bn loans, #3, rebuilding), institutional (WIB) ~17%, Westpac NZ ~12% (NZD-functional, ~18% NZ mortgage share).
  • The transformation thesis – does the multi-year UNITE program (FY26–FY28) close the ~10pp cost-to-income gap to CBA (51.7% vs ~42%, NAB ~43%) and the ~4pp ROE gap (9.8% TTM vs a 10.5% through-cycle anchor)?
  • Rivalry drag – the cost-to-income gap is ~150bps of ROE drag vs the leaders; treated as a management-committed glide toward ~45% by FY29, leaving ~−10bps residual growth drag plus ~−5bps from the business-banking rebuild.
  • Capital – Level 2 CET1 12.42% (Level 1 12.75%), 92bps above the 11.0–11.5% target – binds payout under stress; Total Capital 21.5%, AT1 AUD 8.5bn, total RWA AUD 458bn, mortgage RWA density 22.6%.

worldDesc.Muddle Through: Post-2022 friction proves persistent rather than transitional: inflation cools but lands above target (2.5–3.5%) and central banks tacitly accept the overshoot rather than crush demand. Real rates settle structurally higher than the 2010s (~1.0%). The US keeps outperforming on fiscal expansion, AI investment and immigration, but the lift doesn’t propagate to Europe or EM. Climate policy stays patchy and AI’s productivity transmission is slow, with rents concentrating in platform owners. No crisis, no resolution — a grinding extension of present conditions. Global growth ~2.3%.
worldDesc.Orderly Convergence: The conditions for benign resolution stack up at once. Supply-side normalisation plus genuine AI productivity gains absorb wage pressure, so inflation returns to ~2.3% without a demand crush; real rates settle modestly positive. The political reset climate policy needed happens, and geopolitical tensions materially de-escalate. This time US growth propagates — pulling Europe out of stagnation and supporting EM — and AI rents diffuse, re-expanding growth multiples. Global growth recovers to 3.0–3.2%.
worldDesc.Stagflation Persists: The IMF severe scenario plays out: an energy shock spikes prices and keeps them elevated, inflation expectations break above the 3% credibility threshold, and second-round wage-price dynamics take hold. Central banks lose credibility and hold restrictive policy through the horizon; real rates settle 2–3% with recession inside the scenario. Climate policy backslides as a cost-of-living crisis crushes the transition coalition; growth-stock multiples compress and trade barriers ratchet up. Growth slows to 1.5–2.0%.
worldDesc.Fragmentation: The US-China contest hardens and trade-as-weapon (tariffs, sanctions, export controls) becomes routine, extending into industrial and commodity flows. Supply chains regionalise into duplicated US-aligned and China-aligned systems, energy markets bifurcate, and critical-minerals access becomes the new geopolitical front. The duplicated footprint is inflationary (~3.5%) and growth bifurcates — China-aligned economies may outpace the US-aligned bloc, with Europe hit hardest and Australia facing an acute security-vs-supply dilemma. The new equilibrium is structurally inferior.
worldDesc.Disorderly Climate: The already-running disorderly climate path has its crystallisation moment — most likely a confluence of a catastrophic insured-loss event, regulator-forced de-leveraging of carbon-intensive loan books, and a carbon-price spike. Policy snaps from drift to abrupt crisis action: carbon prices to EUR 200+, border-adjustment mechanisms, expanded transition subsidies. Capital reallocates abruptly, so sectoral dispersion widens sharply even as aggregate growth stays near Muddle Through (~2.0–2.2%, inflation 4.5–5% from carbon pass-through). This scenario tests terminal-state convergence hardest — assumed-perpetual moats reveal stranded-asset half-lives inside the horizon.
worldDesc.AI Productivity Lag: The Solow paradox at AI scale. Capability and capex advance genuinely (deficit-funded, US-led), but economy-wide productivity transformation doesn’t arrive on the bull timeline: enterprise adoption is slow, so aggregate TFP grows only ~0.5% versus the 1.5%+ current investment implies. Rents capture is asymmetric — platform owners take the bulk while broad enterprise pays without proportional payback — and market concentration intensifies. The saving grace is the labour-cost channel: AI contains white-collar wage growth even where productivity transmission is weak. Headline numbers resemble Muddle Through, but the underlying story differs.

_drtheory: Risk-free rate

A long-dated government bond yield in the cash-flow currency, ideally matched to the horizon/duration of the cash flows. Practice splits between the deep, liquid 10-year benchmark and a term-matched long bond for very long-life assets; a single YTM is only an average and distorts NPV when the curve is steep. Most take a recent spot rate rather than a normalised one.

In practice, valuers use a recent spot yield on a long government bond in the cash-flow currency — most commonly the 10-year, though some duration-match to 20 or 30-year bonds for very long-life assets. Normalising the rate is debated but usually set aside in favour of a current market yield.
10-year Commonwealth Government Securities YTM, 4.30% (indicative, May 2026). Single spot 10-year — the pragmatic-benchmark choice.
Equity risk premium

The unobservable expected excess return of equities over the risk-free asset, estimated from long-run historical premia, forward-looking/implied models, or surveys — none theoretically superior. Convention has settled near 6.0%, while acknowledging large statistical error.

Independent experts and practitioners typically adopt a market risk premium around 6.0% (a 5–7% range is common), close to updated long-run historical estimates. The estimate carries very wide statistical error — the true premium behind a measured 6% could plausibly sit anywhere in a 2–10% band — and Australian practice usually makes no explicit imputation adjustment inside it.
5.0% — a Damodaran-style mature-Australia premium, ~100bps below the 6.0% Australian-expert convention.
Beta

Raw single-stock regression beta is noisy and window-dependent, so triangulate from a comparable set: unlever peer equity betas to asset betas and re-lever to a target structure, and/or use adjusted (mean-reverting) or fundamental betas. Index choice (local vs global) and estimation window materially change the answer.

Standard practice is to triangulate from a comparable set rather than trust a single regression: a subject’s measured beta can swing widely across data providers and estimation windows (often anywhere from ~0.8 to ~2.7 for the same company), so experts lean on adjusted / fundamental betas and peer clusters, and treat mechanical unlever / relever with caution.
Peer triangulation: CBA 0.80 / NAB 0.72 / WBC 0.73 cluster → 0.75; ANZ 0.57 excluded as an institutional-dilution outlier, MQG 0.88 a different archetype. Measured 0.73 documented alongside.
Cost of debt / debt margin

Risk-free rate plus a debt margin set by the company’s (or comparable-set) credit rating, referencing traded corporate-bond spreads over sovereigns at matching tenor; use a target rating consistent with the assumed gearing, not just the current coupon.

Cost of debt is normally built as the risk-free rate plus a credit-rating-based margin — a BBB issuer’s traded spread over the sovereign at matching tenor, using a target rating consistent with the assumed gearing rather than the current coupon. Margins of ~1.5–3% over the risk-free rate are typical for investment-grade names.
Not applicable — a bank is discounted at cost of equity, with deposits and wholesale funding treated as operating inputs, not financing (§15).
Gearing / capital-structure weights

Weight equity and debt at market value, using a target/through-cycle structure informed by the subject’s own gearing plus the comparable-set average, rather than a single spot snapshot (which is volatile and often inconsistent with the betas measured over the same window).

Weights are taken at market value on a target / through-cycle basis, informed by the comparable-set average rather than a single spot snapshot — commonly 15–25% debt for capital-light industrials, higher for infrastructure-like assets.
Not applicable — no WACC / EV bridge for a bank.
Gamma / imputation credits

Australia’s dividend-imputation system gives resident investors franking credits; some argue these should be captured via a ‘gamma’ factor (contested, ~0.25–0.65). Regulators such as the AER apply it through the tax line.

Whether to capture franking credits (via a ‘gamma’ factor, contested at ~0.25–0.65) is heavily debated. Many independent valuers decline to adjust for imputation in a business-valuation context, arguing credit value is effectively binary across the shareholder base (full value to some domestic investors, nil to foreign ones) and not reliably priced by the market.
Not applied — consistent with the standard business-valuation view and our imputation-neutral ERP.
WACC vs cost of equity

For an industrial/miner, discount ungeared after-tax cash flows at a WACC, then bridge enterprise value to equity via net debt. For a bank, debt is raw material (deposits/wholesale funding are operating inputs), so discount cash flows to equity at the cost of equity directly — a WACC/EV bridge is wrong.

Industrials and miners are valued by discounting ungeared after-tax cash flows at a WACC and bridging to equity via net debt; concluded WACCs for mature resource / industrial businesses commonly land around 7–9% (higher in higher-risk jurisdictions). Banks are the exception — deposits and wholesale funding are operating inputs, so bank cash flows are discounted to equity at the cost of equity directly, with no WACC / EV bridge.
Cost of equity 8.05% (Rf 4.30% + β 0.75 × ERP 5.0%), held constant across scenarios, no WACC/EV bridge — the bank convention (§15).

narr.Muddle Through:
Post-2022 friction persists without crushing demand. The plasma franchise resumes its secular 5–7% Ig path once the near-term Behring trough (Medicare Part D redesign + China access soft patch) annualises across FY26–27. Vertical integration and fractionation scale hold the margin edge; peer-gap closure delivers +150 bps to Behring by FY31 (full +250 reserved for the upside). Terminal margin 30%, g 3%.

Why ~93% above market? Not because the cash-flow path is heroic — the near-term lines sit on top of consensus — but because the terminal capitalises a high-quality compounder at ~22× forward earnings while the market trades CSL at ~11×. The entire gap is a disagreement about the terminal, not the next two years. Per §16 this premium is a cause for curiosity, not a calibration error: the §3.5.7 reverse-DCF shows no single lever reconciles to market (it would need β ≈ 1.7, or a terminal margin ~half FY25’s, or perpetual −4% contraction), so β is deliberately held at 0.85 to keep the framework rules-based and the gap visible.

Mental short-cut: CSL is a margin story, not a volume story — in every scenario the plasma keeps flowing, so watch the gap between what CSL pays US donors and what Medicare lets it charge. The framework prices the recovery; the market prices the trough.
narr.Orderly Convergence: Inflation re-anchors, real rates normalise, and a productivity surprise eases costs. That buys CSL a faster Behring-trough exit and genuine donor-wage relief, making the full +250 bps peer-gap closure credible. Terminal margin 31.5%, g 3.25%. Instructive that the upside is only +16% — a defensive staple has no operating-leverage explosion; the upside is quiet compounding in a kind world.
narr.AI Productivity Lag: Foundation models advance and gains concentrate in platform owners, showing up as white-collar wage containment — a mild tailwind on CSL’s ~USD 1bn G&A and USD 1.4bn R&D. But softer macro pulls terminal g to 2.875%. The two roughly offset — the tech axis barely touches a plasma franchise. −2.6% vs Muddle Through.
narr.Disorderly Climate: Disorderly transition; carbon-cost pass-through runs inflation 3–5%. CSL is exposed through cost, not demand: fractionation is energy-intensive and distribution is cold-chain dependent, so margins compress. The one genuine portfolio offset sits here — Seqirus pandemic / health-disruption optionality lifts vaccine demand — which is why this lands better than Fragmentation despite the larger cost shock. Terminal margin 28%. −14.2%.
narr.Fragmentation: Trade barriers harden, supply chains localise, and China access becomes a geopolitical instrument. CSL’s collect-in-US / fractionate / distribute-globally model is structurally awkward when blocs fragment, and Behring’s China Ig access is the most exposed line. Peer-gap closure stalls to zero and tax drifts to 20%. With no offsetting segment (unlike the Seqirus climate cushion), the channels compound. −17.4% — the second-worst.
narr.Stagflation Persists: The downside boundary and the clearest illustration of the thesis: plasma demand still holds, so the entire stress arrives as margin — US donor-collection wages surge (supplier-power channel at full stretch), payors press hard on price, and peer-gap closure reverses (Behring margin 150 bps below the FY25 base). Terminal margin 26.5%. Revenue is near-indistinguishable from Muddle Through; the whole 21% fall is the donor-vs-payor squeeze. Even here the number sits +52% above market — the puzzle §16 turns to.

_forces.intro: CSL spans three archetypes (plasma-derived therapies ~72%, vaccines, specialty pharma), so the industry rating is summarised across them. The company offsets are the Behring decomposition — Seqirus and Vifor sit at industry average.
rows: Payers (Medicare, EU health systems, hospitals) hold the purse, but the products are life-sustaining so volume is inelastic — the pressure is on price, with US Medicare Part D redesign the live front.
Same payer mix as peers; no CSL-specific pricing edge
Plasma is collected from paid US donors; supplier power is generally low but donor-collection labour is a real, cyclical cost lever exposed to US frontline wages.
Owns the largest plasma-donor collection network — vertical integration lowers input dependence
5–10yr FDA/EMA/TGA approval plus multi-billion fractionation capex make plasma near-unenterable; vaccines and specialty are low–moderate.
No CSL edge beyond the shared industry moat
No recombinant immunoglobulin at scale and biosimilar plasma is very hard; mRNA and gene therapy are a long-tail, industry-wide risk, not a near-term substitute.
Long-tail risk affects all fractionators equally
A rational oligopoly (CSL / Grifols / Takeda / Octapharma / Kedrion) competing on supply reliability and yield rather than price; capacity is added deliberately.
Scale leader → lower marginal cost via fractionation efficiency
_forces.net: +15 bps margin (supplier +5, rivalry-scale +10), 0 bps revenue growth. CSL captures the industry’s secular growth (Ig demand, indication expansion) plus a modest structural margin edge — but transmits macro stress through margin, not volume.

csl._position:
• Three businesses on one balance sheet: CSL Behring (plasma-derived therapies, ~72% of revenue, ~42% margin), CSL Seqirus (influenza vaccines, ~14%, ~47% margin — demerger announced FY26), CSL Vifor (iron-deficiency / renal specialty pharma, ~14%, ~49% margin, acquired Aug 2022).
  • Franchise edge: the world’s largest plasma-collection network + fractionation scale + FDA/EMA/TGA barriers — a manufacturing / scale moat, not a patent moat (patent-cliff exposure very low).
  • Geography / currency: global USD-functional group, ASX-listed AUD parent; US is ~55% of the plasma market. First worked example where the parent itself is USD-functional.
  • Demand character: price-inelastic in volume (life-sustaining Ig) — scenarios transmit through margin and policy, not volume.
  • Key risk: US Medicare Part D redesign (~USD 100m Ig hit in 1H26) and China Ig/albumin access; donor-collection wage inflation is the other margin channel.
  • Capital: net debt ~1.8× EBITDA and de-levering; USD 750m buyback; Strategic Transformation targeting >USD 500m pre-tax savings by FY28.

A single cost of equity 8.75% is applied to FCFF rather than a blended WACC — a simplification worth flagging; it slightly understates the discount rate versus a formal WACC.
